rationale: A wins because it knows the difference between an angle and a launch dressed up for applause: 'Plaid gives merchants a route around interchange' has a real sub-beat, a same-day peg, and the proof list a reporter will demand. B has good bones, but 'Bank-to-bank payments have flopped at checkout before' asserts a history the update did not supply, then hands the sourcing problem to the journalist. A also says the useful ugly thing: 'Without merchant reaction this is a vendor announcement with a hostile headline on it.'
gaps_in_A: 'FedNow adoption stories have mostly been about disbursements and B2B' is outside context, not supplied evidence. Source it or soften it.
'The prevailing belief in the category is that pay-by-bank is a general-purpose card replacement' risks building a straw man unless you can prove that is actually the prevailing belief.

'Plaid needs 12,000 banks to help route payments past the fees banks collect' is a strong tension, but bank revenue impact and product opt-in are inferences. A flags that, but the headline still walks close to overclaiming.
gaps_in_B: 'Bank-to-bank payments have flopped at checkout before' is an unsourced history claim. That is not an angle yet; it is homework wearing a headline.
'FedNow policy/infrastructure-adoption angle ... duplicate' throws away a real bank-readiness story. Category shift and rail adoption are not the same protagonist.
'furniture, travel, auto, B2B invoicing' are plausible big-ticket examples, but the update supplied no verticals. Label them hypotheses or cut them.
'evidence of where the account-to-account payments category is heading' is too inflated for a launch with no named merchant and no volume. That is category pundit fog, not proof.
